source_text: Ostendit hoc etiam liber ille, qui Sapientia dicitur, cum verba exprimens impiorum, qui post umbram praesentium retecta beatorum merita contuentur: Vitam, inquit, illorum aestimabamus insaniam; et quomodo, reputati sunt inter filios Dei? [n5] Inde est ergo, quod fidelium perseverantia temporum iniquitatibus contumax, et eligens affligi cum populo Dei magis quam temporalis peccati habere iucunditatem [n6] , ab his qui dicunt: Manducemus et bibamus, cras enim moriemur [n7] , nomine pertinaciae et contentionis arguitur; nihilque magis putatur cautis convenire consiliis, quam degeneris animi famulatum emere, vel infidam momentorum quietem. De hac quippe potissimum ignavorum pectorum vilitate factum est, ut per Ecclesiarum naufragia spurcum manichaeorum dogma velificet. Quia si in his qui sacerdotii munere fungebantur, libera stetisset et virilis auctoritas, traducianorum commenta ut invicta ratio proruit, ita publica contrivisset assensio. Verum cum nihil ab hominibus praesentium amantibus, religione vilius aestimatur, itum est in criminationes Dei; ut nobis necessitas immineret, tam longis disputationibus Deum nostrum, qui est Deus verus, fidelem in verbis suis, iustum in iudiciis, sanctum in operibus approbare [n8] .
pass_a_gloss: That book also which is called Wisdom shows this, when expressing the words of the impious, who after the shadow of present things has been uncovered look at the deserts of the blessed: We were estimating their life, it says, as insanity; and how have they been counted among the sons of God? From there it is therefore that the perseverance of the faithful, stubborn against the iniquities of the times, and choosing to be afflicted with the people of God rather than to have the delight of temporal sin, is accused by those who say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die, by the name of pertinacity and contention; and nothing is thought more to suit cautious counsels than to buy the servitude of a degenerate mind, or an unfaithful quiet of moments. For from this vileness especially of cowardly breasts it has been done that through the shipwrecks of the Churches the filthy dogma of the Manichaeans sets sail. Because if in those who were discharging the office of priesthood a free and manly authority had stood, as unconquered reason overthrew the inventions of the Traducians, so public assent would have crushed them. But since nothing is estimated cheaper than religion by humans loving present things, it has been gone into accusations of God; so that a necessity would hang over us, by such long disputations to approve our God, who is the true God, faithful in his words, just in his judgments, holy in his works.

pass_b_english: The book called Wisdom also shows this, expressing the words of the ungodly who, after the shadow of present things, see the merits of the blessed laid bare: ‘We considered their life madness; and how have they been counted among God’s children?’ (Wisdom 5:4–5). This is why the perseverance of the faithful, resisting the wickedness of the times and choosing ‘to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy the passing pleasure of sin’ (Hebrews 11:25), is accused of stubbornness and contentiousness by those who say, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’ (1 Corinthians 15:32; Isaiah 22:13). Nothing is thought more consistent with prudent planning than buying the servitude of a degraded soul, or the unreliable peace of passing moments. It is chiefly this baseness of cowardly hearts that has allowed the filthy Manichaean doctrine to sail amid the churches’ shipwrecks. If a free and manly authority had stood firm in those exercising the priestly office, public agreement would have crushed the inventions of the advocates of inherited sin just as invincible reason overthrows them. But since lovers of present things value nothing less than religion, they have advanced into accusations against God. We have thus been forced to prove through such lengthy arguments that our God, who is the true God, is faithful in his words, just in his judgments, and holy in his works (Psalm 145:13, 17; LXX/Vulgate 144:13, 17).

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
